q: 1. When a change in length takes place, the strain is known as
explain: Linear strain (or longitudinal strain) refers to the deformation occurring along the axis of the applied force.

q: 2. The change in length due to a tensile or compressive force acting on a body is given by
explain: From $\sigma = E \epsilon$, we get $P/A = E(\delta l/l)$. Rearranging for change in length gives $\delta l = Pl/AE$.

q: 3. Young's modulus may be defined as the ratio of
explain: Young's Modulus (E) defines the stiffness of a material under axial loading (linear stress/linear strain).

q: 4. Modulus of rigidity may be defined as the ratio of
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (G or C) is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain, representing the material's resistance to shearing deformation.

q: 5. Two bars of different materials and same size are subjected to same tensile force. If the bars have unit elongation in the ratio of 2:5, then the ratio of modulus of elasticity of the two materials will be
explain: Since $\delta l = Pl/AE$, and P, l, A are constant, $E$ is inversely proportional to elongation. Thus, $E_1/E_2 = \delta l_2/\delta l_1 = 5/2$.

q: 6. When a bar of length l and diameter d is rigidly fixed at upper end and hanging freely, then total elongation produced in the bar due to its own weight is
explain: The elongation of a prismatic bar due to its own weight is given by $\delta l = \gamma l^2 / 2E$, where $\gamma$ (or w) is weight per unit volume.

q: 7. The deformation of a bar under its own weight is ................ the deformation, if the same body is subjected to a direct load equal to the weight of the body.
explain: Deformation under own weight is $WL/2AE$, while deformation under external load W is $WL/AE$. Therefore, self-weight causes half the deformation.

q: 8. The elongation of a conical bar under its own weight is ................ that of a prismatic bar of same length.
explain: The elongation of a conical bar due to self-weight is $\gamma l^2 / 6E$, which is exactly $1/3$ of the prismatic bar's elongation ($\gamma l^2 / 2E$).

q: 9. The length of a conical bar is l, density w and modulus of elasticity E. The elongation of the bar under the action of its own weight will be
explain: As derived in mechanics, the self-weight elongation of a cone is $\frac{wl^2}{6E}$.

q: 10. Strain rosters are used to
explain: Strain rosettes are a combination of three or more strain gauges used to measure the linear strains in different directions on a surface to determine the state of strain at a point.

q: 11. The extension of a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 to d2 is length l and subjected to an axial pull P is
explain: For a tapering bar, the effective area is replaced by the geometric mean of the end areas, resulting in the formula $\delta l = \frac{4Pl}{\pi E d_1 d_2}$.

q: 12. A rod is enclosed centrally in a tube and the assembly is subjected to a compressive load, then
options: both rod and tube are under compression
tube is under tension and rod is under compression
explain: In a composite assembly subjected to an external compressive load, both components must compress together to maintain compatibility of displacement.

q: 13. When a bar is subjected to a change of temperature and its deformation is prevented, the stress induced in the bar is
explain: Thermal stress is induced in a body when its free expansion or contraction due to temperature change is restricted by external supports.

q: 14. A steel bar 5 m long and 40 mm wide is heated from 15°C to 40°C and it is free to expand. The bar will induce
explain: If a material is free to expand or contract during a temperature change without any restraint, no internal resistance (stress) is developed.

q: 15. A bar of copper and steel form a composite system, which is heated to a temperature of 40°C. The stress induced in the copper bar will be
explain: Copper has a higher coefficient of thermal expansion than steel. When heated, copper wants to expand more but is restricted by the steel, putting copper into compression and steel into tension.

q: 16. The thermal or temperature stress is a function of
explain: Thermal stress is calculated using the formula σ = αtE, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion, t is the temperature change, and E is the Modulus of Elasticity.

q: 17. When a circular bar tapering uniformly from diameter d1 at one end to d2 at the other end, is subjected to an increase in temperature (t), then the thermal stress induced is
explain: For a tapering bar, the stress varies along the length. The maximum thermal stress developed when the ends are fixed is (α * t * E * d1) / d2.

q: 18. The deformation of the bar per unit length in the direction of the force is known as
explain: Linear strain (or longitudinal strain) is defined as the ratio of change in length to the original length in the direction of the applied force.

q: 19. Every direct stress is always accompanied by a strain in its own direction and an opposite kind of strain in every direction at right angles to it. Such a strain is known as
explain: Lateral strain occurs perpendicular to the direction of the applied load. If a bar is stretched, it shortens in its transverse dimensions.

q: 20. The ratio of the lateral strain to the linear strain is called
explain: Poisson's ratio (μ) is a constant for a material within the elastic limit, representing the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain.

q: 21. The ratio of change in volume to the original volume is called
explain: Volumetric strain (εv) is the change in volume (dV) divided by the original volume (V).

q: 22. The volumetric strain is the ratio of the
options: original thickness to the change in thickness
change in thickness to the original thickness
original volume to the change in volume
change in volume to the original volume
explain: Volumetric strain measures the overall deformation of a body in terms of volume change relative to its initial state.

q: 23. When a body is subjected to three mutually perpendicular stresses, of equal intensity, the ratio of direct stress to the corresponding volumetric strain is
explain: Bulk Modulus (K) is the ratio of direct stress to volumetric strain when a body is subjected to equal stresses in all three directions.

q: 24. The ratio of shear modulus to the modulus of elasticity for a Poisson's ratio of 0.4 will be
explain: Using the relation E = 2G(1 + μ). If μ = 0.4, then E = 2G(1.4) = 2.8G. Therefore, G/E = 1/2.8 = 5/14.

q: 25. The Young's modulus of a material is 125 GPa and Poisson's ratio 0.25. The modulus of rigidity of the material is
26. Within elastic limit, shear stress is ___________ shear strain.
explain: According to Hooke's Law for shear, shear stress is directly proportional to shear strain within the elastic limit.

q: 27. Shear modulus is the ratio of
explain: Shear Modulus (or Modulus of Rigidity, G) is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

q: 28. In a bar of large length when held vertically, its own weight produces additional stress. The maximum stress will be
options: at every point of the bar
explain: The top cross-section must support the weight of the entire bar below it, making the stress maximum at the support.

q: 29. If the stress produced by a prismatic bar is equal to the working stress, the area of the cross-section becomes
explain: This refers to the theoretical 'limit of length' for a bar under its own weight; if the self-weight stress equals the allowed stress, any increase in length would require an infinite area to maintain that stress level.

q: 30. The ratio of elongations of a conical bar due to its own weight and that of a prismatic bar of the same length, is
explain: Elongation of prismatic bar = γL²/2E. Elongation of conical bar = γL²/6E. The ratio is (1/6) / (1/2) = 1/3.

q: 31. If all the dimensions of a bar are increased in the proportion n:1, the proportion of maximum stress will increase in the ratio
explain: Stress due to self-weight is σ = γL. If all dimensions increase by n, the new length is nL, so stress becomes n(γL), a ratio of n:1.

q: 32. A member with cross-section A mm² is subjected to a force P N. It is L mm long. The linear strain will be
explain: Stress σ = P/A. Strain ε = σ/E = P/(AE). Strain is dimensionless (mm/mm).

q: 33. Young's Modulus is the ratio of the normal stress to the
explain: By definition, Young's Modulus is the constant of proportionality between normal stress and normal strain within the limit of proportionality.

q: 34. In a composite bar, the load distribution... is based on the assumption that all the materials will have
explain: For composite bars subjected to axial loads, the fundamental compatibility condition is that the change in length is the same for all components, meaning they undergo the same strain.

q: 35. In a Uniaxial tension test on a mild steel bar, the Lueders' lines will be
options: inclined at 45° to the direction of tensile stress
perpendicular to the direction of tensile stress
along the direction of tensile stress
explain: Lueders' lines (or slip lines) appear due to shear failure, which occurs on planes of maximum shear stress, typically inclined at 45° to the axis of tensile loading.

q: 36. The percentage elongation of a material from a direct tensile test indicates
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to undergo significant plastic deformation before rupture, measured by percentage elongation.

q: 37. A tie is a member which
options: is subjected to axial tension primarily
explain: In structural engineering, a 'tie' is a tension member designed to resist forces that pull it apart.

q: 38. The product of Young's modulus (E) and moment of inertia (I) is known as
explain: Flexural rigidity (EI) represents the resistance offered by a beam section against bending deformation.

q: 39. The region of the cross-section of a column in which compressive load may be applied without producing any tensile stress, is known as the core... in circular columns the radius of the core, is
explain: To avoid tension in a circular section (Middle Fourth Rule), the eccentricity must not exceed D/8 from the center, making the radius of the core R/4 (or D/8).

q: 40. Stress in members of statically determinate simple frames, can be determined by
explain: All three are standard methods for analyzing trusses; Method of Joints uses joint equilibrium, Method of Sections uses part equilibrium, and Graphical (Cremona) uses vector diagrams.

q: 41. A principal plane is a plane which carries
options: the given of higher magnitude acting
explain: By definition, principal planes are those on which the shear stress is zero; they only carry normal stresses (principal stresses).

q: 42. A prismatic bar is supported at top and is subjected to its own weight... the total elongation of the bar is given by
explain: The elongation due to self-weight is WL/2AE. Substituting W = ρAL, we get (ρAL)L/2AE = ρl²/2E.

q: 43. The moment of inertia of triangular section b x d, about the base is
explain: Using Parallel Axis Theorem: I_base = I_cg + Ah² = (bh³/36) + (1/2 bh)(h/3)² = bh³/12.

q: 44. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum tensile stress is developed on the
explain: For a simply supported beam under downward loads, the beam sags. This creates compression in the top fibers and tension in the bottom fibers.

q: 45. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress is developed on the
explain: As explained in Q. 296, the curvature causes the top layer of a simply supported beam to shorten, resulting in maximum compressive stress.

q: 46. The ratio of maximum shear stress to average shear stress in the case of a rectangular section is
explain: As noted in Q. 301, the maximum shear stress for a rectangle is 1.5 times (3/2) the average shear stress.

q: 47. For the materials which do not have a pronounced yield point... the yield point is taken to be
options: stress corresponding to 0.2% strain from the stress strain curve
the stress at which the permanent set reaches the value 0.2%
average of ultimate strength and actual breaking stress
explain: For materials like aluminum or high-strength steel, the proof stress (yield point) is determined using the 0.2% offset method.

q: 48. An element is subjected to two normal stress σ1 and σ2... The max shear stress is given by
explain: The maximum in-plane shear stress is equal to half the difference between the principal stresses: τ_max = (σ1 - σ2)/2.

q: 49. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then normal stress on an oblique section... inclined at angle θ to the normal... is
explain: The normal stress on an oblique plane is σ_n = σ cos²θ, where θ is the angle between the normal to the plane and the direction of stress.

q: 50. When a body is subjected to a direct tensile stress (σ) in one plane, then tangential or shear stress on an oblique section... inclined at angle θ to the normal... is
explain: The tangential (shear) stress on an oblique plane is given by τ = (σ/2) sin 2θ.
